title: Microwaves don't cook from the inside out
caption: Your microwave twists water molecules billions of times a second. Here's why the middle of your food stays cold.

lines.text: Microwaves don't cook food from the inside out. That's a myth.
Inside every microwave oven is a part called a magnetron. It turns electricity into radio waves.
Inside it, a magnet bends a stream of electrons into a spinning cloud, and that spin makes tiny metal chambers ring with waves.
Those waves bounce around the metal box, and they flip direction about two and a half billion times every second.
Water molecules are lopsided, with a slightly negative end and a slightly positive end.
So every time the waves flip, the water molecules twist to follow them, like tiny compass needles.
All that twisting and bumping into neighbors turns into heat.
But the waves only reach a couple of centimeters into the food. The center warms up later, as heat spreads inward.
That's why big portions stay cold in the middle, and why the turntable spins: to even out hot and cold spots.
And the metal mesh in the door? Its holes are smaller than the waves, so they can't get out, but light can.

visual.label: wavelength, far bigger than the holes

lines.text: Tip: stir halfway through, and let your food rest for a minute so the heat can spread evenly.
